item.text: {"text":"[AHNS (AAAI 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05191) argues that fixed-hardness negatives can create both false-positive and false-negative problems; adapt hardness during training rather than always selecting the highest-scoring item. Evidence is from collaborative filtering, so transfer to masked BERT4Rec remains a hypothesis. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) directly addresses sequential recommendation: uniform-negative warm-start, efficient approximate global candidate recall, then curriculum-controlled negative ranking. Its motivation closely matches bounded-cost mining: premature hard negatives destabilize training, small candidate pools miss informative competitors, and fixed top-ranked selection provides poor difficulty control.\n\nA practical single-model experiment inferred from these findings: retain masked BERT4Rec, warm up with uniform negatives, then score a fixed-size candidate pool using the current network and gradually introduce moderately hard samples alongside uniform samples. Exclude known training positives; cap or downweight extreme-loss competitors rather than assuming every high-scoring unseen item is certainly negative. These safeguards are hypotheses, not verified false-negative detectors. [A 2024 sequential sampling comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds substantial dataset and popularity-band trade-offs, supporting category-level diagnostics alongside macro validation HR@10. [gBCE research](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) separately identifies sampled-BCE overconfidence and instability; calibration is a potential loss ablation, not evidence that harder negatives improve ranking. Keep one trained BERT4Rec checkpoint per category; only pinned validation results can establish gains for Industrial_and_Scientific and Electronics."}
